questions.q: According to Anthropic's own documentation, what distinguishes indirect prompt injection from direct prompt injection / jailbreaking?
options: Indirect injection means the user themselves is deliberately crafting adversarial input
In indirect injection, the user is trusted, but Claude processes third-party content — web pages, emails, tool results — that contains adversarial instructions planted by someone else
Indirect injection only happens when no tools are involved at all
There is no real distinction; the two terms describe identical attacks
questions.explain: Direct injection/jailbreaking has the user as the adversary; indirect injection comes from third-party content the trusted user's agent reads on their behalf, which is the threat model most relevant to tool-using agents.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say tool access specifically raises the stakes of an indirect prompt injection?
options: Tool access has no effect on the severity of prompt injection

A chatbot that reads poisoned content might just produce odd text, but an agent with tool access can be steered into actually taking a real action — sending data, modifying a record — based on injected instructions
Agents with tools are immune to prompt injection by design
Tool access only matters for direct prompt injection, not indirect
questions.explain: An agent is designed to act on what it reads, not just comment on it, so an injected instruction that reaches a tool-using agent can translate into a real, consequential action rather than just a strange sentence.

questions.q: What is the real, published mitigation this lesson describes for handling third-party content like an inbound email body?
options: Concatenate the raw text directly into the system prompt so Claude can see it clearly
Deliver the content only inside a tool_result block, and JSON-encode it so the untrusted text is wrapped as a string value rather than free-form text that could be mistaken for an instruction
Never show the agent any third-party content under any circumstances
Translate the content into a different language before passing it to Claude
questions.explain: Anthropic's guidance recommends putting untrusted content only in tool_result blocks (never system prompts or plain user text) and JSON-encoding it, since the encoding provides an unambiguous delimiter between data and instruction.

questions.q: Why does JSON-encoding an untrusted string (like an email body) help prevent prompt injection, according to this lesson?
options: JSON encoding deletes any malicious text automatically
It makes the text load faster for the model to process
The encoding makes the untrusted text unambiguously a string value inside a data object, so the model sees it as data to report rather than free text it could mistake for a command to follow
JSON encoding is only cosmetic and has no effect on how the model interprets the content
questions.explain: Escaping the untrusted text inside a JSON string gives Claude a clear structural signal that the content is data, not an instruction — an attacker can't as easily "break out" of that encoding to look like a directive.

questions.q: Besides JSON-encoding and using tool_result blocks, which additional defense from this lesson's checklist directly limits the damage a successful injection could still cause?
options: Applying least privilege / credential scoping (from Lesson 25), so even a successful injection has minimal real access to exploit
Removing all tool_result blocks from the conversation entirely
Giving the agent broader tool access so it has more context
Disabling audit logging to reduce the data an attacker could find
questions.explain: Least privilege doesn't prevent an injection attempt from reaching the model, but it bounds what a successful one could actually do, which is why this lesson lists it alongside input-handling defenses as part of the checklist.
